introduction: Looking for help with the cost of a mobility scooter? The right place to start depends on where you live, your everyday mobility needs and the support available to you. A little preparation can help you find the right route before you spend money or submit an application.

This guide walks through the funding options, documents and practical checks worth knowing first. You will find official starting points for the UK, United States, Canada and Australia, followed by a step-by-step application checklist.

gallery.completeCopy: Choose the official route for your location, check its current requirements and ask what evidence you need before ordering a scooter.

items.title: First, Find Out What “Free” Actually Means
paragraphs: There is no single worldwide application that gives everyone a free mobility scooter. An offer might refer to a grant, insurance coverage, a loan of equipment, a donated scooter or a lease paid for through an existing benefit. These arrangements have different eligibility rules and costs.

Before applying, ask whether the equipment becomes yours, whether you will pay anything and whether an allowance you already receive will be used. This is an independent information guide, not an application portal or a funding provider. The organisations linked below explain how to apply to their own services.

items.title: In the UK: Check Grants and Allowance-Based Leasing
paragraphs: The NHS says mobility scooters are not generally available on the NHS. Its guidance suggests checking whether a charity or grant can help with the cost. A GP, occupational therapist or local support organisation can be a useful starting point for discussing your mobility needs and finding relevant services.

The Motability Scheme is another route for people receiving a qualifying mobility allowance. It uses that allowance to pay for a lease, so it should not be confused with a free scooter that you own outright. Check the scheme's current eligibility requirements, costs and lease terms directly before making a decision.

items.title: In the US: Start With Your Coverage and Treating Provider
paragraphs: Medicare Part B may cover a scooter when it is medically necessary for getting around inside your home and its other coverage conditions are met. Wanting help for outdoor trips alone does not establish eligibility. Medicare requires a face-to-face examination and a written prescription from a treating provider, and the equipment supplier must meet its requirements.

Under Original Medicare, you usually pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible. That makes coverage different from an automatically free scooter. Ask your plan and supplier what applies to you, including any approval requirements, supplier restrictions and remaining costs. If you have a different type of insurance, check that plan's own process.

items.title: In Canada: Look for Provincial or Territorial Support
paragraphs: Equipment support can differ by province or territory. Ontario's Assistive Devices Program, for example, helps eligible residents with the cost of power scooters and other mobility aids. Its process includes an assessment by an occupational therapist or physiotherapist registered with the programme.

Ontario generally covers 75% of the approved cost, while eligible recipients of certain social assistance benefits can receive full coverage of the approved amount. This example is specific to Ontario, not a Canada-wide entitlement. Check the current rules where you live and confirm which suppliers, devices and additional costs are covered.

items.title: In Australia: Ask About the Relevant Equipment Pathway
paragraphs: For NDIS participants, assistive technology funding must meet the scheme's rules and relate to the person's disability support needs. An assessment can explain how the equipment supports their goals, how it works with other supports and what previous equipment they have used.

The NDIS may need supporting evidence, trial information and a quote, depending on the equipment and its cost. Speak to your NDIS contact and a suitably qualified adviser about the correct process. Being interested in a scooter does not by itself establish eligibility, and other support routes may be more appropriate for some people.

items.title: Describe the Everyday Problem You Need to Solve
paragraphs: Before an appointment, write down the situations where getting around is difficult. Include practical examples: reaching essential rooms, travelling to appointments, managing a usual shopping trip or keeping up with activities that matter to you. Describe what happens on a typical day and how your needs vary.

Also note which walking aids or equipment you already use and what they do not help you achieve. Concrete examples give the assessor more useful information than a preferred scooter model alone. Be accurate about your needs and let the qualified professional explain which equipment may suit them.

items.title: Check Who Must Carry Out the Assessment
paragraphs: Different funding routes use different assessment processes. Before paying for a report, ask the funder who is allowed to provide it and whether a referral is needed. A report from the wrong provider may not meet that programme's requirements.

Ask what the appointment involves and whether you should bring a support person, details of your home or information about existing equipment. The purpose is to identify a suitable solution, which could be a scooter, a wheelchair or another form of support.

items.title: Gather the Documents the Provider Actually Requests
paragraphs: Request the official checklist before collecting paperwork. Depending on the route, you may need proof of residence, insurance or benefit details, the required assessment, a prescription or a supplier quote. A charity may ask for financial information if its grant is based on need.

Check that names and contact details are consistent, that reports are current enough for the programme and that every required section is complete. Send sensitive documents only through the verified provider's approved process. This website does not need your medical records or benefit numbers for you to read the guide.

items.title: Try Suitable Equipment Before Choosing a Model
paragraphs: A scooter needs to fit both the person and the places they plan to use it. Discuss steering controls, seating, getting on and off, turning space, storage and charging with the assessor or supplier. Ask for an appropriate demonstration or trial rather than choosing by appearance alone.

Think about transport too. A model that works well locally may be difficult to lift into a vehicle or store at home. Tell the provider about steps, narrow entrances and other access issues so that these can be considered before an order is placed.

items.title: Get the Total Cost in Writing
paragraphs: Ask for a clear quote that separates the scooter, any required accessories, delivery and other charges. Then ask the funder which parts it will cover. Optional upgrades can leave a balance even when the basic equipment is funded.

Also check who pays for servicing, repairs, replacement batteries and insurance if relevant. For a lease, ask about the ongoing payment and what happens when it ends. A written explanation helps you compare the actual arrangements rather than relying on a headline about a free scooter.

items.title: Submit Through the Correct Organisation
paragraphs: Find out who submits each part of the application. You may need to apply yourself, or the process may involve a clinician, approved supplier or support worker. Confirm where the documents go and whether a decision is required before ordering equipment.

Keep copies of forms, quotes and correspondence, together with any reference number. Ask how the provider will contact you if information is missing. Do not assume that buying a scooter first will lead to reimbursement later; check that point directly before spending money.

items.title: Understand What Happens After Approval
paragraphs: Read the written decision and confirm the equipment, approved amount and any contribution you must make. Ask who will arrange delivery and whether setup, fitting or instruction is included. Check the ownership or loan conditions rather than assuming they are the same for every route.

At handover, ask the supplier to explain charging, safe storage, routine checks and the procedure for reporting a fault. Keep the paperwork and contact details somewhere easy to find. If the equipment does not match the agreed specification or seems unsuitable, raise that with the provider promptly.

items.title: If the Request Is Declined, Ask for the Reason
paragraphs: A declined request can have different causes, including missing evidence, a device that does not meet the programme's criteria or a need that belongs under a different service. Ask for the decision and its reasons in writing.

Check whether a review or appeal is available and what deadline applies. If the issue is incomplete information, ask exactly what is missing. An adviser familiar with the programme may help you understand the next step, but a review does not guarantee a different outcome.

items.title: Check Other Support If There Is a Funding Gap
paragraphs: If the main route does not cover the full cost, ask a local disability organisation or recognised charity whether other help is available. Grants, refurbished equipment, loan schemes and short-term hire may be worth asking about, depending on your area and circumstances.

Confirm each organisation's eligibility rules and whether funding must be approved before purchase. For used or donated equipment, ask about suitability, battery condition, repairs and any warranty. A low initial price is only useful if the equipment can meet your needs reliably.

items.title: Verify Offers Before Sharing Personal Details
paragraphs: An advert is a starting point for checking an offer, not proof that you qualify. Verify the organisation through its official website and contact details before sharing insurance numbers, identity documents or financial information. Be especially careful if someone promises guaranteed approval without knowing your circumstances.

Medicare advises people to protect their Medicare number and share it only with trusted people who should have it. It also says Medicare will not call to sell you equipment. Use the official provider's contact route if you are unsure who is asking for your details.

items.title: Your Application Checklist
paragraphs: Before taking the next step, make sure you can answer these questions: Which funding route applies where I live? Who must assess me? What evidence is required? Which suppliers can I use? What will I pay? Do I need approval before an order is placed?

Start with the official links below, confirm the current rules and request the relevant application checklist. The aim is to match a suitable mobility solution with a funding route you actually qualify for, with the costs and responsibilities clear from the beginning.
